setup: To understand Angkor you have to start with water, because the whole civilization is, in the end, an argument about water. Mainland Southeast Asia is drained by a handful of huge rivers, the biggest of them the Mekong, and near the bottom of its run the Mekong does something almost no river on Earth does: every monsoon it backs up so hard that a tributary, the Tonlé Sap, reverses and pours backward into a lake instead of out of it. The lake roughly quadruples, drowns the surrounding forest, then drains, leaving fresh silt and an almost unbelievable quantity of fish. That reversing lake is why a great civilization grew up here, inland, rather than only on the coast — it handed free protein and rebuilt soil, year after year, to whoever could organize the people around it. What this chapter is really about is how that surplus gets organized, and how a bundle of ideas carried up the river from India — Sanskrit, the Hindu gods, the divine king — turned scattered rice kingdoms into the prologue for an empire.

bridge: Chapter 1 left the lower Mekong fertile, populous, literate, and thoroughly Indianized — writing in Indian-derived script, praying to Shiva and Vishnu, crowning its kings with Indian ritual — but politically scattered, and chafing under the influence of a foreign sea power the inscriptions call simply "Java." Chenla, the inland Khmer kingdom, had split into a "Land Chenla" up the river and a "Water Chenla" down by the coast. It was a region waiting for someone to walk up a mountain and declare it whole. A man named Jayavarman is about to.
setup: Every empire has a founding scene, and the Khmer one takes place on a mountaintop in the year 802, when a Brahmin priest consecrates Jayavarman II as a universal monarch and institutes the cult of the devaraja — the god-king — explicitly to make Cambodia "no longer dependent on Java." That is the founding myth, and the honest catch is that almost everything we know about it comes from a single inscription carved 250 years later by a family of priests glorifying their own hereditary office. So this chapter holds two things at once: the structural fact that Khmer kingship fused the ruler with the divine — a king built a temple-mountain housing a god bound up with his own sacred identity, and merged with it when he died — and the genuine uncertainty about what that 802 ceremony actually was, and even what the word devaraja meant. What is not in doubt is the template the early kings set: build a reservoir, build an ancestor temple, build your own mountain for your god.

bridge: Chapter 2 gave the early kings their template: a king proved he was a king by building a reservoir for his people, an ancestor temple for his dynasty, and a state temple-mountain for his god. Jayavarman II had founded the line on a mountaintop and ruled from the lowlands at Hariharalaya; Indravarman I had set the formula in sandstone at Bakong. But the capital was still southeast of the great plain that would one day carry the City. In 889 a new king moves it onto that plain for good, and the formula starts getting bigger.
setup: This is the chapter where Angkor becomes Angkor — the word just means "the City," the Khmer pronunciation of the Sanskrit for city. King Yasovarman I moves the capital onto the plain between the lake and the hills, and the building scales up to match a single overriding idea: every great temple is a stepped pyramid because it is Mount Meru, the cosmic mountain at the center of the universe, built at buildable scale — its towers the gods' peak, its walls the world's mountain ranges, its moat the cosmic ocean. The reservoirs scale up too, into the enormous engineered lakes called barays, among the largest hand-built things in the pre-modern world. But the throne has no firm succession rule, so it is fought over by war, capitals are abandoned and reclaimed, and one question hangs over everything: what were those giant reservoirs actually for — irrigation, the cosmic ocean made real, or both? That argument, scaled up, is the same one about why Angkor eventually ended.

bridge: By now Angkor sits on its plain, building temple-mountains that model the cosmos and reservoirs you cannot see across, all of it justified by the god-king idea Jayavarman II founded the line on. But Chapter 3 also exposed the empire's permanent weakness: no firm rule of succession, so the throne is contestable, and it is contested — by brothers, uncles, usurpers, often by war. Capitals have already been abandoned and reclaimed once. The eleventh century opens, as it should by now not surprise you, with another civil war.
setup: Suryavarman I wins that war after roughly eight years of fighting and settles in for a long, consequential reign doing the unglamorous work: he expands Khmer power west into what is now central Thailand — planting, though no one could know it, the exact ground from which the Thai kingdoms will one day rise and destroy Angkor — and he tries to fix the thing that keeps breaking the state. With no reliable bureaucracy, he has an oath of allegiance sworn by some 4,000 officials and carved into the palace gateway: government by mass loyalty oath, set in stone, because there is no professional machine to do the job. Meanwhile the building goes on — the huge Baphuon temple-mountain, the largest reservoir at Angkor — and so do the revolts. The eleventh-century pattern is stark: grand temple, giant reservoir, expensive wars, armed rebellion at home. The Khmer state is a machine for turning a farm surplus into stone and conquest, and the harder a king runs it, the more it shakes.

bridge: Everything so far has been building toward one monument. The water, the god-kings, the temple as a model of the cosmos, the formula of reservoir-and-ancestors-and-mountain getting bigger every century — Chapter 4 left the eleventh-century state at its most expansive, pushing west into Thailand and converting its whole surplus into stone. The throne, as always, was contestable, and around 1113 a young prince settles the question the Khmer way.
setup: He settles it by murder: Suryavarman II attacks the reigning king, his own great-uncle, and kills him in battle, leaping onto the enemy's war-elephant "as Garuda kills a serpent" — the line is propaganda, but notice that Khmer kingship brags about the seizure rather than hiding it. Then he builds the building on the flag. South of the city he raises Angkor Wat, which is, by enclosed footprint, the largest religious monument ever built — a deliberate, exact model of the Hindu cosmos at colossal scale, with five towers as the peaks of Mount Meru and a moat as the cosmic ocean. It breaks two Khmer rules: it honors Vishnu where almost every temple honored Shiva, and it faces west, toward death, where almost every temple faces east — the leading reading being that it was the king's own funerary temple. He is also an aggressive, outward-facing ruler whose repeated invasions of Champa set up the catastrophe of the next chapter.

bridge: For five chapters this book has shown you the Khmer building: the god-kings, the reservoirs, the temple-mountains, and at last Angkor Wat itself, the largest religious monument on Earth, raised by the aggressive, outward-facing Suryavarman II. He spent his reign attacking his neighbors, among them the coastal kingdom of Champa, and then he died around 1150, probably on a failed campaign, and the throne fell into exactly the contested, weak-handed succession the story keeps warning about. The neighbor he had spent his life bullying had not forgotten.
setup: This is the chapter where the Khmer almost stop existing. The Cham were a maritime people on the central Vietnamese coast, speaking an Austronesian language as far from Khmer as an Englishman is from a Malay sailor — and being a sea power, they could do what no land enemy could. In 1177 a Cham fleet came by water: up the Mekong, across the great lake, falling on the capital from the lake side by surprise. They took the city, killed the king, burned Yasodharapura, and then did not leave — for roughly four years Champa occupied the heartland of Angkor. This is the hinge of the whole book, the single greatest "almost": in the timeline where 1177 is permanent there is no Bayon, no hospitals, no Angkor on a flag. Everything that follows happens only because one royal prince, already in his late fifties and out of power for years, emerged from obscurity to organize the resistance — and to beat a sea power that came by river, he had to win on the river.

bridge: Chapter 6 was the hinge: in 1177 a Cham fleet sailed up the rivers and across the great lake, sacked Yasodharapura, killed the king, and occupied the heartland of Angkor for roughly four years. The empire that had built the largest temple on Earth was, suddenly, a defeated territory of a maritime rival it had spent decades bullying. It was reversed by a royal prince already in his late fifties, who emerged from obscurity, beat the sea power on the water of the lake itself, and was crowned around 1181 over a burned and recently occupied capital. He is, if this book has a protagonist, the man.
setup: Jayavarman VII was already roughly sixty when he became king, and in the next forty years he built more of Angkor than every king before him combined. The deepest thing he changed was the idea of the king himself. For nearly four centuries Khmer monarchs had been Hindu god-kings fused with Shiva or Vishnu; Jayavarman VII was a devout Mahayana Buddhist, and he recast kingship as a bodhisattva-king — a ruler whose sacred role was not to be a god but to relieve his people's suffering. That reframing was also a building permit: a god-king builds a temple for his divine essence, but a bodhisattva-king builds hospitals, roads, rest-houses, reservoirs, and a whole walled city, and calls all of it compassion. Out of it pours the most ambitious public-works program in Khmer history — Angkor Thom, the haunting face-towers of the Bayon, temple-towns the size of cities — and, shadowing it all, the argument that has run since Chapter 4: was it too much?

bridge: Chapter 7 ended on the empire's greatest king and a nagging accusation: Jayavarman VII built more of Angkor than everyone before him combined — Angkor Thom, the Bayon, hospitals and roads and temple-towns — and converted the entire surplus into stone for forty years, and the "exhaustion thesis" says that effort broke the empire. He died around 1218, and after him no king ever built on that scale again. But the empire did not fall over when its greatest builder died. It kept going, populous and rich, for a long time, and this chapter is about that city at its height — and about a quiet change already dissolving it from inside.
setup: Here is the corrective: the single best description of Angkor as a living, glittering, functioning city comes from after the supposedly ruinous Jayavarman VII, and it comes from one foreign tourist. In 1296 a Chinese envoy named Zhou Daguan arrived with a Mongol-Yuan mission, stayed about eleven months, and wrote a short book — the only detailed eyewitness account of daily life inside the Khmer Empire that exists. Everything textured we can say about how Angkorians lived, traded, ate, married, and judged crime comes substantially from this one observant outsider. He describes a wealthy, hierarchical city where the traders were surprisingly women, a brutal justice system, and the reversing lake of Chapter 1 still feeding one of the largest concentrations of people in the pre-modern world. But underneath the glitter the religious ground had already shifted: Theravada Buddhism was spreading from below, and Theravada has no use for a god-king, no need for a Mount Meru in sandstone or an army hauling stone. That, more than any enemy, is the worm in the apple.

bridge: Chapter 8 described thirteenth-century Angkor at its glittering height through Zhou Daguan's eyes — a populous, wealthy city the supposedly ruinous Jayavarman VII had not killed off at all. But it also pulled the worm out of the apple: Theravada Buddhism was spreading from below, village monastery by village monastery, and Theravada needs no god-king, no Mount Meru in sandstone, no corvée army hauling stone. The last great royal Sanskrit inscription dates to 1327; after it, the brahmin-Sanskrit court culture that had run the empire for five centuries simply goes quiet. The religious reason to build the way Angkor built had evaporated.
setup: The most important fact in this chapter is something that stopped: after Jayavarman VII no Khmer king ever built another great stone temple, and the silence in the stone after about 1220 is the clearest evidence the civilization had become something else. This chapter is about everything that went wrong on top of that, over the two slow centuries it took for "the capital is here" to become "the capital is somewhere else." The external threat had a name the Khmer had planted themselves — Tai-speaking peoples founded kingdoms on the very western frontier Suryavarman I had conquered, first Sukhothai and then, far more dangerously, Ayutthaya in 1351, which took Khmer statecraft and ritual and turned the whole apparatus against its teacher. Siamese campaigns hit Angkor again and again, and in 1431 an Ayutthayan army took the city and the court did not move back. But the textbook framing of "the fall of Angkor" is wrong in two ways this book has been preparing you to see.

bridge: Chapter 9 dismantled the textbook story of a sudden 1431 "fall." The Ayutthayan sack was the loudest event in a two-century retreat already underway — the temple-building had stopped around 1220, Theravada had dissolved the god-king economy from below, and the court was sliding south toward the rivers and the booming maritime trade. And the most famous thing people think they know is a myth: Angkor was never abandoned. The capital moved, the population thinned, but Angkor Wat itself was converted into a Theravada monastery and continuously tended by monks, with Khmer kings and Japanese pilgrims still visiting. This final chapter is about where the "lost city" myth came from — and the harder question it was always covering up.
setup: This chapter has two jobs. First, the still-unsettled argument about what actually happened to Angkor, because it is the textbook case of "civilizational collapse" and the textbook has been substantially rewritten in the last fifteen years. The old hydraulic-city thesis — the aging waterworks silted up and the civilization failed under its own infrastructure — has not survived intact; tree-ring data published in 2010 revealed the 1300s and 1400s swung between severe multi-decade droughts and violent monsoons, close to a worst case for a society that was one long bet on managing water, while a rival argument says there was no collapse to explain, only a relocation and a religious transformation. The honest consensus is multi-causal and undramatic: several pressures converging, no one of them destiny. Second, the temples' afterlife from 1431 to now — the European visitors, Mouhot's "discovery" that discovered nothing, the French archaeologists and the looters, the Khmer Rouge, and the lasers that, flown from 2007, stripped away the forest digitally and revealed a city far larger than anyone had guessed.
